message.reasoning:
I need to make a Monopoly decision.

I am p2 with $1035 and only one opponent left. I control the dark blue and red monopolies with four houses on each. The opponent has $363 and is at GO.

The opponent controls the brown monopoly with four houses on each property. Their greens are incomplete.

I am calculating the opponent's liquidation value. Their cash increased to $363 after passing GO, raising their total assets to roughly $1393.

Selling the eight brown houses would raise cash to $563. Mortgaging properties would add more funds, but selling houses is the fastest way to pay a debt.

The opponent's total liquidity is $1393. Park Place rent of $1300 is now affordable, so that property no longer threatens bankruptcy. Boardwalk rent of $1700 still exceeds their assets, meaning it does. I am weighing my next move.

Building a hotel on Park Place would raise rent to $1500. That exceeds the opponent's $1393 liquidity and would bankrupt them. Boardwalk would need a $2000 rent to kill them, but that is too expensive. I am checking whether the even-build rule allows replacing four houses with one hotel.

The even-build rule allows one hotel while the other property keeps four houses. I have enough cash to build a hotel on Park Place for $200, leaving me with $835. That would raise rent to $1500 and bankrupt the opponent. I am now considering whether to also upgrade Boardwalk for another $200.

Boardwalk hotel would not change the kill, but it would reduce my cash buffer. I am now mapping the board to assess the risk of landing on the opponent's brown properties.

I mapped the squares from Vermont Avenue. The opponent's unmortgaged Electric Company and Penn Railroad are the only rent threats ahead. Virginia has no monopoly, so its rent is only twelve dollars.

I am now considering the opponent's next turn from GO. Their first landings are Mediterranean and Baltic, both with four houses. I have no rent threat from this side.

The opponent cannot reach my dark blue properties in one roll from GO. A Chance card that advances them to Boardwalk would land them on Boardwalk with four houses and bankrupt them.

I checked the red properties. Illinois rent with two houses is three hundred dollars, and even a hotel would be one thousand two hundred seventy-five dollars. Indiana and Kentucky are cheaper still. None of these can bankrupt the opponent, so only the dark blues remain as threats.

I cannot reach Baltic Avenue next turn from Vermont. The opponent would need to pass almost the entire board to land there. I still have a full orbit of risk ahead, but it is not immediate.

The opponent would need roughly five to six turns to reach Park Place from GO. That delay gives me time to land on their properties first.

My remaining danger zones are Baltic Avenue at nine hundred dollars, Mediterranean Avenue at four hundred fifty dollars, and utilities or railroads at manageable amounts.

I am now factoring in the income tax and luxury tax. Keeping my full cash of $1035 would leave me with $135 after paying Baltic Avenue's $900 rent. Building a hotel on Park Place would drop my cash to $835, which is too low to cover that rent without selling a house. Selling one Boardwalk house for $100 would raise my cash to $935, but that still leaves only about sixty-five dollars short of the $900 needed. I am weighing whether the extra rent from the hotel is worth the risk of needing to sell a house.

I am recalculating the opponent's liquidity more carefully. I listed standard mortgage values for all their properties and totaled the unmortgaged mortgageable value at $830.

The opponent's total assets are exactly $1393. A Park Place hotel would bankrupt them by $107, while a Boardwalk hotel would bankrupt them by $307. Even with three houses on Boardwalk, the margin is only seven dollars. I am now checking whether they could sell a Get Out of Jail Free card to raise cash.

If the opponent sells a Get Out of Jail Free card for fifty dollars, their liquidity rises to $1443. A Park Place hotel would still bankrupt them, but three houses on Boardwalk would no longer do so. I will keep Boardwalk at four houses and build the hotel on Park Place for two hundred dollars.

Building a hotel on both dark blue properties would cost four hundred dollars and leave only six hundred thirty-five dollars cash. A hotel on Boardwalk alone would not improve the kill, since it already bankrupts the opponent. A hotel on Park Place alone costs two hundred dollars and leaves eight hundred thirty-five dollars cash. That is the only upgrade that matters.

I checked whether selling a red house would break the even-build rule. Indiana and Illinois each have two houses, so I can sell one for seventy-five dollars to cover Baltic Avenue's nine hundred dollar rent. That leaves enough cash without touching the dark blue properties.

I rejected upgrading Kentucky to two houses because it would not kill the opponent. Unmortgaging the light blue properties would cost over one hundred twenty dollars in interest, and even four houses on those streets would still leave rent below the opponent's liquidity. The orange set is similarly too weak to threaten bankruptcy.

I ruled out trading with the opponent. They would not agree to weaken their own holdings, and I already have enough power to bankrupt them without deals. I confirmed that building a hotel on Park Place is a single action.

Mortgaging raises cash without paying interest. I checked the bank's hotel supply and confirmed there are enough for a replacement. I also noted that building a hotel on Park Place would reduce my total house count from thirteen to nine.

I verified that street repairs are affordable even after building the hotel. I will post a short public message about the upgrade and keep the detailed reasoning private.
